items.body:
Landsec, owner of one of the UK’s leading retail and leisure portfolios, has expanded its partnership with the retail industry charity the Retail Trust to support employees at its shopping destinations affected by abuse at work.
Through the Retail Trust’s Let’s Respect Retail campaign to tackle abuse, Landsec piloted free resilience and de-escalation training at four of its major shopping destinations in 2025 and 2026. The practical sessions gave hundreds of people the skills and confidence to manage challenging interactions and recover quickly after difficult moments on the shop floor.
This month, the Retail Trust’s support will be rolled out across a further 13 Landsec destinations across the UK*, ensuring retail staff, cleaners and security and guest services teams, from Glasgow to Portsmouth, get the help they need when experiencing challenges at work.
Everyone working at a Landsec shopping destination will be given access to new online tools from the Retail Trust on the Landsec Protect app to help them stay safe, respond to difficult situations and recover afterwards. This includes new advice on how to respond to issues like antisocial behaviour and being filmed without consent or targeted after a shift.
There will also be more face-to-face support ranging from new staff training to meetings with retail managers to help them protect their teams.
The partnership is being expanded as the British Retail Consortium’s 2026 Crime Report reveals that retail workers face more than 1,600 incidents of violence and abuse every day, with 43,000 physically violent incidents per year. The newly introduced Crime and Policing Act has now made the assault of a retail worker a standalone criminal offense in England and Wales – further underlining the significance of the issue.
Throughout the remainder of 2026, The Retail Trust’s Let’s Respect Retail materials will be visible across Landsec’s shopping centres. More than 300 businesses backed the campaign last year by displaying messages in stores and shop windows asking people to treat their staff with kindness and the Retail Trust and Landsec will be once again calling on shoppers to act respectfully in the run up to this Christmas.
A security guard who took part in the training earlier this year said: “When you’re dealing with antisocial behaviour or difficult customers, it can stay with you even after your shift has finished and you can feel anxious about coming back into work the next day.’’
“The training was really useful because it showed that people across different roles are dealing with many of the same challenges, and that there is support available from the Retail Trust. The coping techniques were practical and there was something in there that could work for everyone.”
“This is going to become even more important coming up to Christmas, when there are going to be more shoppers, more pressure and more temporary staff who may not have dealt with these situations before. Support like this gives people more confidence to know how to respond and how to look after themselves afterwards.”
Bruce Findlay, managing director of retail at Landsec, commented: “Everyone has the right to feel safe and respected at work. Our industry depends on the millions of people working in our place and abuse should never be accepted as simply part of the job.
“At Landsec and across our UK-wide destinations, we believe it’s vital we do everything we can to ensure difficult situations don’t become the norm or deter people from joining and staying in our industry. That’s why we’re extending our partnership with the Retail Trust to increase access to training and support for people working in the shops, restaurants and keeping our places clean and secure. And we’re asking everyone who visits our destinations to play their part in ensuring retail workers feel respected and valued. If the people at the heart of our places feel supported, it should lead to better experiences and more reasons for our guests to smile.”
Chris Brook-Carter, chief executive of the Retail Trust, said: “The people who’ve taken part in our training tell us that thoughtless, unkind and aggressive behaviour can stay with them long after their shift has ended and that they increasingly worry about situations like filming by shoppers or being targeted outside of work. We’re working with Landsec to give thousands of staff working at its shopping destinations more support while reminding millions of shoppers to treat everyone with respect.
“We all have a role to play in creating more respectful and kinder shopping environments and our charity’s Let’s Respect Retail campaign will remind us all that even something as simple as a greeting or a smile can make a huge difference to people who are facing daily hostility at work.”

The Cotswold Company, the digitally-led premium handcrafted furniture and homeware brand, has launched a curated collection of made-to-last furniture with Marks & Spencer, further extending its omnichannel reach and creating opportunities to introduce the brand to new customers.

Orders will be fulfilled via the Cotswold Company’s Cotswold Home Delivery – the Group’s specialist white-glove delivery service carried out by highly trained delivery experts to confidently handle any delivery challenges, offering total peace of mind to customers.

items.body:
Waitrose Clapham Junction today (Thursday 17th September at 8am) welcomes customers back through its doors, following an extensive transformation designed to deliver an upgraded, modern shopping experience for south London food lovers.
The opening marks a fortnight of significant investment in the area, following the reopening of nearby Waitrose Balham on Friday 11th September, which also underwent a comprehensive store transformation.
To mark the Clapham Junction reopening, celebrations will take place across the morning with live musical entertainment at the shop entrance, alongside a special pop-up sampling station to treat local commuters and shoppers. In-store, the first customers through the doors will be greeted with a complimentary glass of prosecco or orange juice, and a commemorative reusable Waitrose tote bag for their groceries, with even more food and drink tastings taking place throughout the weekend.
The shop, located on St John’s Road, has undergone a comprehensive nine-week refit to introduce an array of enhancements, modernised departments, and operational improvements that celebrate quality food and seamless service.
Key highlights of the Clapham Junction transformation include:
- New dry-aged beef cabinet: A culinary destination for home cooks, the new cabinet showcases the finest British cuts.
- New customer coffee machine: Shoppers can now treat themselves on-the-go to a hot drink from a dedicated self-serve station – the perfect perk for local commuters and myWaitrose members.
- Smoother, intuitive store layout: Redesigned aisle flow to make browsing effortless – whether popping in for tonight’s dinner or doing the full weekly shop.
- New refrigeration: replaced for improved energy efficiency.
Branch manager, Martin Lockwood, who leads the team of 85 Partners at Waitrose Clapham Junction, said: “Our Clapham Junction branch has been at the heart of the bustling St John’s Road community for almost 20 years, and this refurbishment is all about giving our customers the inspiring experience they deserve.
“From our new-look layout to our product displays, every improvement has been made with our customers in mind.
“Hot on the heels of our sister store in Balham reopening just last week, this is a real demonstration of Waitrose’s commitment to our south London community. We’re thrilled to welcome everyone back with live music, giveaways, and plenty of delicious food to taste.
“On behalf of all the Partners here at Clapham Junction, we want to say a huge thank you to our loyal customers for their patience. We can’t wait to show you around your new shop.”
Gary Burt, executive BID manager for Clapham Junction Business Improvement District, added: “We’re delighted to see Waitrose on St John’s Road reopen following an extensive refurbishment. We believe the significant investment in this project signals a clear vote of confidence in Clapham Junction as a destination town centre.
“Waitrose has always played an important role in Clapham Junction, providing local employment, attracting visitors and offering products and services that enhance the customer experience.
“The refurbished store further complements the rich mix of independent and high-street businesses on St John’s Road and strengthens Clapham Junction’s reputation as a vibrant and welcoming destination for residents, workers and visitors alike.
“We’d like to congratulate the Waitrose team on this exciting milestone and look forward to the positive contribution it continues to make to our local economy and the Battersea community.”
Nationwide investment
Waitrose is committed to investing in its estate, including nationwide refurbishments and new openings. This forms part of a £1bn, multi-year programme designed to offer the very best products, service and shops for customers.
This month has also seen refurbishments of stores in Finchley and Balham, and Waitrose is on track to open three new stores this year – two full-line supermarkets in Hale Barns (Greater Manchester) and Cricklewood (North West London), and a convenience store in Ascot (Berkshire). Waitrose is refurbishing 28 shops this year and launching into airport travel retail for the first time with four RELAY stores in Heathrow Terminal 2.

items.body:
Launching this September, Zizzi’s Christmas advert will mark their first TV advertising campaign since November 2021 and forms part of the brand’s wider investment in building brand salience ahead of the key Christmas trading period.
The return to TV and digital advertising comes at a significant point for the brand, following a major menu revamp last year which has driven strong customer feedback and NPS scores. The campaign aims to remind consumers that, whatever their dietary requirements or preferences, there is a place for everyone at Zizzi.
The creative brings this insight to life through Santa as the ultimate Christmas host, as he attempts to organise the annual Santa Christmas meal. As the plans get underway, his phone starts filling up with messages from the other Santas, each with their own dietary requirements and preferences. From vegan and gluten-free requests to those who simply can’t eat certain ingredients, Santa is faced with the familiar challenge of trying to make sure there is something for everyone.
The result is a humorous take on the often unspoken pressure that comes with organising a Christmas meal. While the guests might be thinking about what they want to eat, the person organising it is thinking about whether everyone will be happy.
It is a human insight that sits at the heart of Zizzi’s ‘Merry Zizzi EVERYONE’ proposition, showcasing the brand’s ability to cater for different tastes and dietary needs without anyone having to compromise. Zizzi’s menu includes options for vegetarian, vegan and non-gluten diners.
The campaign represents Zizzi’s largest media investment in three years, underlining the brand’s renewed focus on building awareness and consideration at a key trading period for the restaurant sector.
The first campaign burst will run through to mid-October, before returning in November and December to support the key Christmas booking and dining period. The campaign will be supported by Zizzi’s wider Christmas activity across PR, social, influencer and in-restaurant channels.
George Whiting, head of marketing and communication at Zizzi, said: “Great campaigns start with a human insight, and we all know that person who takes on the job of making sure everyone is happy at Christmas. We wanted to bring that to life in a fun and relatable way, while showing that whatever your tastes or dietary requirements, Zizzi has a place for everyone. Following the success of our menu revamp and excellent NPS score, it felt like the perfect time to bring Zizzi back to TV.”
The campaign comes as Zizzi looks to drive Christmas bookings and consideration while reinforcing its position as a restaurant where everyone can come together, whatever their food preferences or dietary requirements.
Zizzi’s Christmas set menu will be available from 17th November, with two and three course options priced at £24.95 and £29.95 respectively.

Ben Reilly has been appointed operations director, following 21 years with the Group, most recently as head of property and […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! items.body:
The Beaverbrooks Group, which owns jewellery and watch retailer Beaverbrooks and luxury watch and fine jewellery boutique retailer Loupe, has strengthened its director team with three senior appointments, increasing the team from five to seven.
Ben Reilly has been appointed operations director, following 21 years with the Group, most recently as head of property and store design. Jo Wilkinson becomes digital and brand experience director, bringing more than 15 years’ experience and continuing to lead the Group’s omnichannel and digital development. Nick Bucknell, who has spent 22 years with the Group, becomes watch buying and Loupe operations director, taking responsibility for watch buying across the Group alongside his existing Loupe and Rolex responsibilities.
The changes strengthen the Group’s leadership structure while recognising the experience and contribution of long-standing members of the team. This includes Adelle Thompson, who joined Beaverbrooks in 1978 and remains the company’s director of jewellery buying and merchandising. The Adlestone family’s ownership of Beaverbrooks remains represented by the third generation, with Mark Adlestone OBE continuing his close involvement in the business as chairman and director. Beaverbrooks and Loupe will continue to develop their respective retail, digital and customer experiences, while focusing on being an exceptional employer.
Simon Smith’s role will evolve from retail director to retail, people and culture director, continuing the Group’s increased focus on its people, culture and retail development.
The changes also mark the beginning of the retirement of Roger Fairhurst, who will step down as brand director at the end of September after more than 35 years with the Group and will leave the business in spring 2027. During his long tenure, Fairhurst held various positions within the retail side of the business, before moving to Beaverbrooks’ head office where he was instrumental in the development and success of Beaverbrooks’ e-commerce function.
Anna Blackburn, managing director at Beaverbrooks, said: “We are delighted to welcome Ben, Jo and Nick to the director team. All three have built long and successful careers with The Beaverbrooks Group and bring significant expertise across our business.
“This is an exciting time for the Group and the right moment to strengthen our leadership team as we continue to deliver our strategic vision and work towards our core purpose of enriching lives.
“We are also incredibly grateful to Roger for more than 35 years of commitment to the business and everything he has contributed throughout his career.”
For further information about Beaverbrooks, visit: beaverbrooks.co.uk

items.body:
This September, Gü is expanding its chilled desserts portfolio with the launch of its Pâtisserie Sharing Range – a brand-new product concept designed to bring premium pâtisserie-style dessert to the sharing category.
Designed to serve 6-8 people, the range taps into growing demand for premium desserts that can be enjoyed as part of social occasions and at-home entertaining.
Distinct from Gü’s cheesecake range, the new collection combines indulgent layers, an irresistibly oozy centre and a delicate sponge base to deliver a premium sharing experience.
Launching with three flavours available all year round – Zillionaire Pâtisserie, Spanish Lemon Pâtisserie and Salted Caramel Pâtisserie – the range offers an entirely new way to enjoy the signature flavours Gü fans know and love, reimagined in a sophisticated and more elevated sharing dessert.
Zillionaire Pâtisserie layers double chocolate ganache, treacle-infused 
Spanish Lemon Pâtisserie combines lemon curd, lemon crème and lemon confit with delicate sponge for a bright, citrus-led offering to the range.
Salted Caramel Pâtisserie features layers of caramel crème, vanilla crème and buttery French salted caramel over a delicate sponge, transforming a much-loved flavour into a dessert designed for slicing, serving and sharing.
The launch will be supported later in the year by two limited edition festive variants – White Chocolate & Raspberry Pâtisserie, combining white chocolate ganache and crème with raspberry compote and sponge, and Gingerbread Caramel Pâtisserie, which brings together warming gingerbread spice, caramel, sponge and vanilla crème.
Each dessert comes complete with a bespoke Gü Slicer tool, enabling consumers to serve clean, even portions that showcase the product’s layers.
Fred Ponnavoy, head chef at Gü, says, “Creating the Gü Pâtisserie collection was about taking the flavours people already love from Gü and reimagining them in a format designed for sharing. I’m always thinking about how flavours and textures work together, and this range gave us the opportunity to bring those much-loved combinations to life in a new way. From rich chocolate and caramel to bright citrus and festive flavours, every dessert has been carefully crafted to deliver the layers, textures and indulgence people expect from Gü, while bringing people together to enjoy and share something special.”
The all year round formats of the Gü Pâtisserie Sharing Range launch in retailers from 14th September 2026, RRP £9.99 (prices at retailer’s discretion). The limited-edition festive variants will launch exclusively through Sainsbury’s later in the season with an RRP of £12 (prices at retailer’s discretion).

items.body:
A.F. Blakemore has welcomed a new retailer into the Spar estate through its Blakemore Trade Partners plus offering with the opening of Spar Tutbury. This is an unusual site as it takes a standout conversion and brings one of the village’s most recognisable buildings back into community use.
The store is owned by Kalpesh Odedra, an experienced retailer within a family-run business. Kalpesh purchased the site as a freehold and has undertaken a sensitive redevelopment of the former Lloyds Bank which closed in March 2022, and the Swinkles Family Brewers office that followed. The building has been empty since 2024, and its Art Deco frontage, original front doors, safe door and vault have all been retained to create a store with genuine architectural character and a unique customer experience.
Spar Tutbury has been designed to serve basket-shopping missions, with a range tailored to local needs and a focus on fresh food, value and everyday essentials. The store offers a premium wine and spirits range, dedicated Free From, Gluten Free and Vegan sections, and strong value through the County Bridge 3 for £9 fresh meat offer and Fresh Savers fruit and veg range. A fresh Indian street food counter, including sweets, and a serve-over ice cream bar provide a distinctive food-to-go experience not previously available in the village. The store will also offer a 12 week price promise on key essential lines through Price Lock until autumn.
Kalpesh Odedra said: “This building has always meant something to local people, and we wanted to bring it back into everyday use in a way that genuinely supports the community. Spar’s focus on fresh food, everyday value and reliable service means we can offer Tutbury a store that feels welcoming, familiar and built around what shoppers need. Our aim is to create a place the village can be proud of and to keep this beautiful building alive for many years to come.
We chose BTP+ because it gives independent retailers the support, structure and confidence to deliver a stronger store for their community. The programme makes it easy to focus on fresh food, value and the right ranges, while still keeping the individuality of the site. For a building as unique as this one in Tutbury, BTP+ has helped us bring the space back to life in a way that feels modern, reliable and genuinely customer-focused.”
Taranjit Dhillon for A.F. Blakemore said: “This is an exceptional building and Kalpesh has done a remarkable job in bringing it back to life. Spar Tutbury is a perfect example of how heritage sites can be reimagined for modern convenience retailing, and we are delighted to support this development.”
The opening has created new employment opportunities and strengthens SPAR’s presence in Staffordshire.
Spar Tutbury is now open to customers.

Peacocks and Bonmarché are focussed on investing in their store estate and opening new stores in key retail locations. items.body:
Fashion retailers Peacocks and Bonmarché are growing their ‘store within a store’ partnership with Co-op, opening six new concessions this month which takes the total together to 20.
Peacocks and Bonmarché are focussed on investing in their store estate and opening new stores in key retail locations. The latest development sees four new Peacocks stores opening inside Co-op stores located in Cranleigh (Surrey); Machynlleth (Powys, Wales); Kippax (Leeds) and Whitby (North Yorkshire) – taking the total number of Peacocks concessions operating within Co-op stores to 13.
In addition, Co-op is welcoming two new branches of Bonmarché which open in its Lampeter (Ceredigion, Wales) and Shotts (North Lanarkshire, Scotland) stores this month, the new stores follow the opening of four* Bonmarché concessions inside Co-op stores earlier this year – taking the total to seven.
Co-op is committed to creating stores with added services, which are a destination locally, and the ‘store within a store’ concept brings new shops, jobs and consumer choice to enrich high streets and communities. The move also enables the fashion retailers to bring their latest collections to more communities, showcasing the latest range of inspirational fashion, everything from wardrobe essentials and fashion staples to nightwear, accessories, and footwear.
The Bonmarché stores feature exciting collections from their brand ambassadors, Lisa Snowdon and Lorraine Kelly, as well as their everyday luxury brand Dash and casual lifestyle brand Autonomy.
Whilst Peacocks includes new collections from celebrity ambassadors Dani Dyer, Louise Redknapp and Michael Owen, and fashion for all the family with the new Dani Dyer Mini Collection for children.
Amanda Waterfield, Bonmarché retail director, commented: “We’re delighted to announce the opening of further Bonmarché concessions within Co-op stores in Lampeter and Shotts – following the successful launch of four branches inside Co-op stores earlier this year.
“This new ‘store in store’ concept allows us to showcase our full fashion offering, including our latest collections and exciting celebrity collaborations.
“We’re excited to become part of these new communities and offer customers stylish womenswear at exceptional value. This partnership also reflects our continued investment in the local high street, with over 225 Bonmarché stores across the UK, and we want to give a huge thank you to all the teams involved.”
Sharron Lamb, retail director at Peacocks, said: “We’re so excited to open a further four Co-op concessions stores across the country, adding to the seven the new Peacocks stores we have opened this year, so far.
“With our new Autumn ranges, classic Christmas pjs and winter accessories available in-store now, shoppers can be sure to get everything they need to get ready for the new season at Peacocks.”
Kevin Buchan, head of partnerships, Co-op, said: “We are delighted to grow our partnership with Peacocks and Bonmarché, and to work with them to unveil their latest in-store concessions. Co-op is committed to backing high streets and communities, and we work to ensure our stores are more than just a shop. We aim to create a destination in communities combining great quality products, value and deals along with a compelling range of added services – all at the heart of local community life.
“Providing a home for Peacocks and Bonmarché inside the local Co-op enables them to bring their latest value fashion collections to more communities, at the same time providing a new store, employment opportunities and additional consumer choice, locally.”

Following today’s release of Next’s figures for the six months ending 1 August 2026; Louise Deglise-Favre, lead apparel analyst at GlobalData, a leading intelligence and productivity platform, offers her view: “Next continues to credit the hot weather for its strong H1, but its lasting outperformance is the result of a well-executed strategy, centred on improved […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
Following today’s release of Next’s figures for the six months ending 1 August 2026; Louise Deglise-Favre, lead apparel analyst at GlobalData, a leading intelligence and productivity platform, offers her view: “Next continues to credit the hot weather for its strong H1, but its lasting outperformance is the result of a well-executed strategy, centred on improved product offerings, strong value for money credentials and international expansion. H1 FY2026/27 sales rose 9.0%, as consumers continued to respond well to Next’s superior value for money credentials. While Next upped its full year full-price sales guidance from 6.3% to 6.7% and profit before tax guidance from £1,243m to £1,255m, the uplift remains conservative as the retailer still expects a slowdown in H2, in both UK online sales and international sales. However, Next has a history of underestimating its future performances, so it would not be entirely surprising if it beats this somewhat conservative guidance once again.
“In the UK, Next’s sales rose 4.5% in H1, driven by the online channel which rose 8.0%, while store sales fell 0.4%. Within the UK, Next’s own brand full price sales fell 0.5%, mainly due to declines in store, which could not fully be offset online. While this drop was expected against the strong comparatives boosted by the disruption at M&S last year, it also indicates that Next has some improvements to make in its own product lines. The retailer has identified its menswear line as an opportunity for growth but does not anticipate its refreshed product ranges to have an impact until H2 next year. In the meantime, Next will have to count on its LABEL division to drive growth, which should not be too much of an issue as full price sales of wholly-owned brands and third-party brand rose 32% and 10% respectively in H1. However, this reliance on third-party brands might prove risky in the long run as more players pivot towards a marketplace multi-brand model, increasing competition. Having a strong own-brand range will likely be key for differentiation in the future.
“Online international sales rose 26.4% in H1, helped by pent-up demand in the Middle East in Q2 after disruptions from the war in Iran in Q1. The retailer also started to see meaningful growth in the US, though the territory remains a small portion of its revenue. However, Next is expecting to see a slight slowdown in sales in H2, as comparatives in Europe become much stronger from August onwards given this is when it started using Zalando’s fulfilment arm ZEOS last year.”

items.title: Next warns Burnham against 'stifling growth' with tax hikes as it upgrades profits again
items.summary: The fashion retailer, which has been run by Lord Wolfson since August 2001, warned that increases at the upcoming 28 October Budget could worsen weak consumer confidence.
items.body:
Next warns Burnham against 'stifling growth' with tax hikes as it upgrades profits again
- See more This is Money on Google - save us as a Preferred Source
Next has warned the Government against 'stifling growth' with tax hikes as the retailer upgraded its profit forecast for the fourth time this financial year.
The fashion retailer, which has been run by Lord Wolfson since August 2001, warned that any tax increases in the upcoming 28 October Budget could worsen weak consumer confidence.
Wolfson's comments came as Iceland boss Richard Walker also urged Andy Burnham to stop treating business as a ‘piggy bank’.
Further tax rises would spell bad news for the economy and exacerbate worries about rising inflation, higher mortgage rates and a bad jobs market, Wolfson said.
He added: ‘The tax burden is at its highest level for over 60 years and seems to us to be at the point where further increases only risk stifling growth – and lower growth is likely to only worsen Government finances – a vicious circle.
Next has warned it expects its UK sales growth to see a 'modest' slide over the rest of the year.
'In our view, the best outcome for UK growth would be a credible plan to get Government spending under control – eliminating the fear of higher taxes – alongside supply side measures to boost growth.’
Next said there was likely to be a ‘modest’ reduction in its UK sales growth for the rest of the year. It predicts sales growth of 2 per cent for the final six months of 2026, compared to a previous forecast for 2.8 per cent.
But Wolfson said the sales decline would be a ‘slow, steady decline as the year progresses’ rather than a ‘precipitous decline.’
Retailers, including John Lewis and Frasers, have already urged the Government to not fund business rates reductions for pubs by whacking up the rates paid by large shops.
Lord Richard Walker, who runs frozen food chain Iceland, also told LBC: ‘Andy Burnham has been Father Christmas so far, and it would be great if he'd start to get a bit more unpopular... We cannot, for the sake of all of us, keep taxing business and view it as some piggy bank that can constantly be raided.’
The gloomy remarks came as Next wowed investors again with the fourth profit upgrade this year after better than expected trading in the UK and overseas this year so far.
The company operates around 458 shops in the UK and Ireland, which employ more than 20,000 workers.
Pre-tax profits soared 10.5 per cent to £569 million in the six months to July. The business now anticipates annual profits will rise 8 per cent to £1.23 billion, compared to a previous forecast of 7.3 per cent. Sales are now expected to jump 6.7 per cent.
This was because UK full price sales rose 3.6 per cent, thanks to 7.4 per cent growth online offsetting a 1.7 per cent fall in stores.
The group recently withdrew from the race to buy ailing department store Harvey Nicks, which was picked up by rival retail giant Frasers. Next owns other labels including Reiss, FatFace, Joules, Cath Kidston, and Made.com, plus joint ventures running Victoria's Secret UK and Gap UK.
The retailer admitted it ‘could be doing better’ in some areas, including menswear, which posed ‘the biggest opportunity’.
It comes as rival Marks & Spencer has also been attempting to poach more of the menswear market with collaborations with celebrities including David Gandy.
Next said that its menswear ranges ‘became too focused on multiple variants of essentially the same item, serving the same customer’ after holding onto bestsellers ‘for too long’.
It has revamped some ranges but only expects to see ‘marked improvement’ until the second half of next year.
Some of its other brands have also lacked new products and styles and the business is keen to expand its menswear licenses.
Wolfson also said that consumers prefer ‘the authentic creativity of human beings’ compared to designs generated by Artificial Intelligence.
He said: ‘When it comes to artwork and colour, outstanding aesthetics require a human hand, creative eye and an emotional response. That means we are putting more emphasis on designers using techniques that connect them directly to the artwork – painting, drawing, screen printing, etc.’

items.title: Next forecasts bigger profits after hot weather lifts sales
items.summary: FTSE 100 retailer, which owns UK rights to US brands Gap and Victoria’s Secret, says prices could rise in autumn Business live – latest updates Next has thanked warmer weather for an “unexpected” boost in sales, leading the clothing retailer to raise its profit forecasts for the fourth time this year. The FTSE 100 company, which owns the UK rights to the US brands Gap and Victoria’s Secret as well as stakes in labels including Reiss and Joules, raised its expectations for full-year profits by £12m to £1.26bn. Continue reading...
items.body:
Next has thanked warmer weather for an “unexpected” boost in sales, leading the clothing retailer to raise its profit forecasts for the fourth time this year.
The FTSE 100 company, which owns the UK rights to the US brands Gap and Victoria’s Secret as well as stakes in labels including Reiss and Joules, raised its expectations for full-year profits by £12m to £1.26bn.
It is the fourth time Next has raised profit forecasts this year, with the company having last ratcheted up its expectations in early August, as Europe faced a series of heatwaves.
Next, which has more than 500 stores across the UK, said in a stock market update on Thursday: “The first half was much better than we originally anticipated, both in the UK and overseas.
“It is important to acknowledge that part of this overperformance has been the result of two unusually warm summers in the UK. The rest of the overperformance is, we believe, largely the result of fulfilling the aims we outlined at the beginning of the year.”
That has included some cost-cutting efforts, particularly across Next’s warehouses.
Overall, total sales across the group were up 9% in the six months to July, helping push pre-tax profits for the half-year up by 11% to £566m.
Next said the performance over the past six months was “all the more unexpected given the strength of sales last year”. It made £1bn of annual profits for the first time last year.
However, the retailer cautioned on the impact of the rising cost of living and prospects for the jobs market.
“Our primary concerns are rising inflation, higher mortgage interest costs and a weak employment market. These worries will only be compounded if they are accompanied by tax increases,” it said, in an apparent reference to John Healey’s first budget on 28 October.
“It seems likely that it [the government] will have to increase taxes in order to fund its expenditure.”
While the group said it was deploying AI across the business, including its tech division, Next said it was ensuring fashion designs were still led by humans.
“In a world where AI is able to do more and more, our experience suggests that consumers prefer the authentic creativity of human beings,” it said. “That means we are putting more emphasis on designers using techniques that connect them directly to the artwork – painting, drawing, screen printing, etc. That is a big investment in time, and requires a higher level of creative talent than is needed to operate CAD [computer aided design] or prompt AI.”
Aarin Chiekrie, an equity analyst at Hargreaves Lansdown, said: “Next delivered its first-half results in style, with sales growth accelerating over the period and breezing past the fashion company’s original guidance. In the UK, hotter-than-expected weather and more effective marketing saw customers logging in to refresh their summer wardrobes online, helping offset a small decline in-store.”
Shares rose 2% in early trading on Thursday, making Next the top riser on the FTSE 100.

items.title: Wickes boss tells Andy Burnham to make it easier to hire young people again as it plans new stores
items.summary: David Wood, the chief executive of the DIY retailer, has echoed calls from other retailers for Andy Burnham to ease the costs associated with part-time and entry-level roles.
items.body:
Wickes boss tells Andy Burnham to make it easier to hire young people again as it plans new stores
- See more This is Money on Google - save us as a Preferred Source
The boss of Wickes has become the latest retail chief to urge the Government to make it easier to hire young people.
David Wood, the chief executive of the DIY retailer, echoed calls from major retailers for Andy Burnham to ease the costs associated with part-time and entry-level roles.
It has become ‘twice as expensive’ to employ someone compared to two years ago, Wood told The Times.
He added: ‘Making it more affordable to employ would be helpful, and also maintaining the ability for us to manage a flexible workforce. Not only are 30 per cent of our colleagues in store aged 16 to 24, 45 per cent of them work on part-time hours because it suits their life.’
His remarks came after he revealed group revenues rose 2.1 per cent to £865.3million in the six months to the end of June, despite a difficult economic backdrop.
The business said it also expects to have opened four to five new stores and refurbished 12 stores by the end of the year.
Wickes plans to reach 300 stores and has also invested in digital sales, which it said had helped a significant improvement in trading.
Jobs drive: David Wood called for the Government to make it easier to hire young people
It said its customers have not been ‘immune’ from cost-of-living pressures, including increased mortgage rates and energy costs.
But they ‘tend to be slightly older and more affluent than the UK average’, which has protected its sales while the rate of housing transactions ‘remains stable’.
Wickes reported profits before tax of £24.6million for the six months, up 1.7 per cent on the same period a year earlier, and it expects to meet market expectations with profits before tax up 10 per cent this year.
Youth unemployment has reached worrying levels amid a crisis of 16-24-year-olds who are ‘not in education, employment, or training’ – so-called NEETs.
In her first Budget in 2024, former chancellor Rachel Reeves increased the employer National Insurance contribution rate from 13.8 per cent to 15 per cent and reduced the secondary threshold to £5,000.
This caused fury among retail and hospitality firms because it dragged many part-time and lower-paid staff into the tax for the first time.
Bosses have also complained after inflation-busting increases to the minimum wage over the past two years have driven up staff costs.
The Wickes boss's comments come as Brewdog co-founder James Watt also hit out at the Prime Minister and said he should ‘get out of the way’ and help bosses by reducing the costs.
The entrepreneur, whose craft brewery business collapsed in March and was sold to US firm Tilray, criticised Burnham for stating that jobless youth have ‘been let down by an education system that told them there was only one route to success, and then left them without the opportunities to get their foot in the door anywhere else'.
Watt said that the Prime Minister ‘missed the mark’ and was not taking ‘ownership’ of its own role in making it less appealing for employers to hire young people.
He added: ‘There is also something deeply ironic about the government blaming “the system”, as though the Government is somehow separate from it, whilst all this Labour government has done is make it increasingly difficult and more expensive for businesses to employ people.’
The remarks echo those of Asda boss Allan Leighton, who last month said the Budget was an opportunity for the new Prime Minister and Chancellor to shift away from a model of heavy taxes on business which inhibits growth to one that enhances it.
'This is a real tipping point: instead of just talking about growth, the government now has an opportunity to change tack and actually make growth happen,’ he said.
Just weeks ago, High Street retailers urged John Healey to roll back Rachel Reeves’ employer National Insurance raid to ‘turn the tide’ on unemployment.

items.title: Next lifts profit targets but sounds alarm on ‘vicious circle’ of high tax and low growth
items.summary: Next has lifted its profit target again following “much better” than expected trading in the first half of the year as the retailer was spurred on by booming international sales and record summer temperatures. The FTSE 100 retail giant saw sales across its group jump by nine per cent in the six months to July, [...]
items.body:
Next lifts profit targets but sounds alarm on ‘vicious circle’ of high tax and low growth
Next has lifted its profit target again following “much better” than expected trading in the first half of the year as the retailer was spurred on by booming international sales and record summer temperatures.
The FTSE 100 retail giant saw sales across its group jump by nine per cent in the six months to July, as it posted a £569m pre-tax profit, 10.5 per cent higher than last year.
The retailer told shareholders: “The first half was much better than we originally anticipated, both in the UK and overseas. […] The performance in the first half is all the more unexpected given the strength of sales last year.”
Next posted a 7.4 per cent uplift in UK online sales, compared to its previous guidance of 4.6 per cent, as in-store sales declined by only 1.7 per cent – a softer fall than the 3.3 per cent it had expected.
The group said it now expects to make a full-year pre-tax profit of £1.26bn because of higher-than-expected sales and cost savings in its warehouse operations. This is the firm’s fourth profit upgrade this year.
Lord Simon Wolfson, the firm’s chief executive, said: “It is important to stress that the progress we have made is not the result of a carefully drawn up strategy devised in the boardroom and dutifully implemented across the group.
“Next is not a command-and-control operation. Our overall ambitions are very clear, but they are fulfilled, and to some extent shaped, by hundreds of initiatives and decisions taken by colleagues across the group.”
Labour must ‘get spending under control’
The group’s sales growth in the first half of the year was lifted by a 24 per cent boost in its international sales, while total UK sales edged up by four per cent.
Sales of the Next brand in the UK fell by 0.5 per cent, or £7m, which the group attributed to the growth of its third-party brands, which are “likely to have had some adverse impact on Next brand sales”.
The group has snapped up a number of smaller retailers in recent years, including Joules, FatFace and Russell & Bromley.
Next said that the “great success that the [Next brand] enjoyed” at the start of the decade “encouraged us to hold on to bestsellers for too long”. The retailer is planning to boost the “newness,” choice and quality of its menswear range to grow sales, it said.
Ahead of October’s Budget, retailers have urged Andy Burnham’s government to back the high street by cutting business rates and to tackle youth unemployment by slashing employment costs.
Next said the government’s huge debt and high level of public spending means it “seems likely that it will have to increase taxes” next month.
“In our view, the best outcome for UK growth would be a credible plan to get Government spending under control – eliminating the fear of higher taxes – alongside supply side measures to boost growth,” the group said.
Next cut its outlook for UK sales growth in the final six months from 2.8% to 2% as it flagged concerns over the impacts on consumer spending from the rising cost of living, higher mortgage costs and a cooling labour market.
Lord Wolfson said: “The tax burden is at its highest level for over 60 years and seems to us to be at the point where further increases only risk stifling growth – and lower growth is likely to only worsen Government finances – a vicious circle.”
Aarin Chiekrie, an equity analyst at Hargreaves Lansdown, said: “Next delivered its first-half results in style, with sales growth accelerating over the period and breezing past the fashion company’s original guidance.
“In the UK, hotter-than-expected weather and more effective marketing saw customers logging in to refresh their summer wardrobes online, helping offset a small decline in-store.”
Shares in Next gained 2.4 per cent to 14,915p in early trading.

items.body:
WorkJam announces expansion of tie up across portfolio of JCPenney’s parent company Catalyst Brands
WorkJam, a frontline operations platform, is expanding its partnership with department store JCPenney, part of the Catalyst Brands portfolio. This covers every brand in the Catalyst portfolio group, including Aéropostale, Brooks Brothers, Lucky Brand, and Nautica, and brings WorkJam's platform to approximately 70,000 associates across North America.
"Serving millions of customers across our unmatched portfolio of iconic brands depends on creating a workforce that is connected, agile, and increasingly AI enabled,” says Andre Joyner, EVP and Chief Human Resources Officer at Catalyst Brands. "We believe the future of work will be defined by how thoughtfully organisations use technology to help associates perform at their best.”
“Through our partnership with WorkJam, we're embedding AI directly into the flow of work, giving associates faster access to needed information, reducing everyday friction, and creating more capacity for managers to lead their teams and serve customers. This expansion reflects our commitment to enabling our talented workforce while deploying AI responsibly and at scale, with the associate experience at the centre of everything we do."
As part of the expanded partnership, Catalyst Brands is also launching WorkJam's AI Agent, bringing conversational, on-demand HR support to employees across all five brands directly within the WorkJam app. Employees can get answers to HR and benefits questions in their own words, in the moment, reducing the need to contact support centres or pull managers off the floor. As the AI Agent is built into the WorkJam platform, it can provide policy-based information while respecting the permissions and governance controls that apply to the WorkJam experience.
Catalyst Brands plans to expand the AI Agent over time, extending it beyond HR support to help employees with everyday operational questions in the flow of work.
"Catalyst is expanding WorkJam across all five brands because it's delivering for their associates and the managers who lead them," says Steven Kramer, CEO at WorkJam. "As part of that, they're putting AI directly in the hands of employees, starting with on-demand HR support, inside the same platform they already use to run their operations. This gives employees fast, conversational access to HR information where they work, while providing Catalyst with a foundation to expand AI powered support across the frontline over time."

AI will be a key focus area at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards.

Congratulations to our winners, and a big thank you to our sponsors, judging panel, the legend that is Tiff Stevenson, and all those who attended our 2025 gathering.

Costco expands delivery on Uber Eats platform across USA bringing quick commerce service to 47 states
Uber Technologies and Costco have announced an expansion of their US partnership, bringing Costco delivery through Uber Eats to customers in 47 states, up from 17. Nearly 600 of the retailer’s locations are now available on the on demand delivery platform.
This includes locations in Arizona, California, Connecticut, Illinois, Michigan, New York, and Pennsylvania. Costco’s full inventory of items - from bulk paper goods and groceries to its line of Kirkland Signature products, including the fan favorite $5 rotisserie chicken - is available for delivery.
“We are thrilled to expand our partnership with Costco nationwide, giving Costco members more ways to shop and bringing the brand’s storied selection and value to more consumers,” says Andrew Macdonald, President and Chief Operating Officer at Uber. “Costco is one of the largest and most trusted retailers in the country for good reason, and our nationwide partnership demonstrates the scale and opportunity Uber can bring to retailers looking to meet more of consumers’ everyday shopping needs.”
In addition to the US, Costco is also available on Uber Eats in Canada, Mexico, Japan, Taiwan, France, and Spain.
Instacart
Earlier this year, Instacart and Costco Wholesale announced the expansion of their North American partnership into Europe, with the launch of Costco’s first ever same-day delivery websites in France and Spain, powered by Instacart’s Storefront Pro commerce platform and fulfillment solutions services.
Costco members in France and Spain can now shop online and receive delivery through its websites in each country. The initial roll-out includes delivery from all locations in France and Spain, including the Paris metropolitan area and Mulhouse in France, as well as Bilbao, Madrid, Seville, and Zaragoza in Spain.
Orders are fulfilled and delivered from the store to the member’s door. Instacart is teaming with European partner companies in each country at launch for the picking, packing and delivery of orders. Members will also be able to get same as-in-store pricing.

Instacart is included in RTIH’s first ever Retail Technology Hot 100 List. Launching in August, this sees us bringing you the hottest companies whose solutions and systems are helping drive the retail sector forward.

These companies operate across the omnichannel retail landscape (stores, online, mobile, supply chain, payments etc).
Our judging panel, including Vineta Bajaj, Group CFO, Holland & Barrett, Dan McGrath, JD Group Customer Operations, JD Sports, Dr. Astha Purohit, Director of Product Management, Customer Data and Identity, Walmart, and Paula Bobbett, Chief Data and Digital Officer, Boots, provided feedback on those who have the most innovative, forward thinking technology offerings and are also best addressing retailers' current challenges, painpoints, and opportunities.
The judges used the following framework when making their picks:
1. Retailer problem fit - how meaningful, strategic, and widely felt the retailer pain being addressed is.
2. Production traction in retail (2025–2026) - real named retailer deployments, pilots. 
3. Innovation and defensibility - genuine technical novelty paired with a defensible competitive position.
And there was also a public vote, with thousands of members of our community of retail tech enthusiasts getting involved. Thanks to all those who took part! Based on the judging panel's feedback and the public vote, we then drew up our first ever RTIH Retail Technology Hot 100.
So, without further ado, here are the 100 hottest global retail technology ventures right now. Drum roll, please…

European Media Marketplace appoints industry veteran Christophe Parcot as Non-Executive Chairman
The European Media Marketplace (EUMM) has announced the appointment of Christophe Parcot as Non-Executive Chairman. Parcot brings more than 25 years of experience across the European technology, media and advertising ecosystem.
He has held senior leadership positions, including Head of Yahoo EMEA, global COO of Teads and Ogury, and CRO of Solocal (Yellow Pages). He is currently a Senior Advisor to McKinsey and to B2B European scale-ups as the founder of consultancy Sixt5 Partners. He has contributed to the EUMM working group since its inception.
In his role as Non-Executive Chairman, Parcot will support the coalition's governance and strategic direction, helping build alignment across its community of media owners, data companies, telcos, retailers, marketplaces, and advertising technology partners. He will also represent the coalition externally and support the expansion of its ecosystem as the marketplace moves from its launch to execution and wider market adoption.
Launched in summer 2026, the European Media Marketplace gives advertisers, according to a press release, “first-party data as well as direct access to premium supply across the open web (display, video, CTV and retail media) cutting unnecessary intermediary costs while improving revenue for European media and data owners”. The first founding partners include T Advertising Solutions (part of Deutsche Telekom), Equativ, Experian, lastminute.com, leboncoin and Kleinanzeigen (part of Adevinta), Orange Advertising (Orange France), Vinted, and Vodafone.
“Europe has no shortage of strong premium media, data and technology companies,” says Parcot. “The challenge is bringing that strength together in a way that can compete at scale. The European Media Marketplace was created with that ambition. The next step is to turn the model into something tangible for advertisers, agencies, and media owners: more direct access, distinctive audience data segments, and ultimately more value for every advertising euro. That means testing the proposition in market and proving the value it can deliver through real campaigns. With the foundations now in place, our priority is clear: move from ambition to execution.”
Arnaud Créput, CEO at Equativ, says: "Building the European marketplace has reinforced one of my strongest convictions: collaboration only works when every partner has an equal voice and nobody tries to control the outcome. That is why independent governance matters so much. Christophe has the experience and credibility to protect that spirit as we grow, challenge us when needed, and keep us focused on creating together what none of us could build alone."
Satya Vinnakota, Business Director of Ads at Vinted, comments: “The right leadership is required to align so many different stakeholders, from data owners and brands to adtech providers and publishers. items.body:
How AI is reshaping what Irish consumers expect from everyday digital services
Ireland has quietly become one of Europe's more AI literate countries. The European Commission's 2026 Digital Decade Country Report, confirmed by the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment earlier this month, ranks Ireland fifth in the EU for generative AI adoption at 45%, well above the EU average of 33%, and second for basic digital skills, with 83% of the population reaching at least a basic level. This isn't a country still finding its feet with new technology.
That comfort with AI has spilled into ordinary digital life well beyond the chatbots themselves. Streaming platforms suggest what to watch next, online shops nudge you toward things you didn't know you wanted, and entertainment platforms increasingly let people build out their own corner of a much bigger catalogue, whether that's a tailored playlist or customised game libraries like PlayOJO casino. Personalisation has gone from a feature worth mentioning to something people simply assume is there.
Personalisation Is Now the Baseline, Not the Bonus
For years, personalisation online meant a handful of "recommended for you" tiles stuck on a homepage. It's a good deal more layered than that now. Recommendation engines don't just look at what you bought or watched last week, they pick up on browsing patterns, time of day, even how long you lingered on something before scrolling past. E-commerce sites use this to shorten the gap between browsing and buying. Streaming services use it to stop people getting stuck flicking through menus. Done well, most users barely notice it's happening at all, which is really the point of it.
That shift matters because it's changing what people expect as a baseline rather than a bonus. A recommendation that feels random, or a search that turns up pages of irrelevant results, now reads as clunky rather than merely average. You'll hear a similar complaint about customer service too. People have far less patience for being passed between departments or repeating themselves to a new advisor, when so many everyday interactions, from a banking app flagging unusual spending to a retailer sorting a delivery query through a chat window, now happen instantly and with some sense of context already built in.
Where AI Does Its Quietest, Most Useful Work
Financial services are a useful example of AI doing quiet, largely invisible work. Fraud detection systems flag suspicious transactions in real time. Budgeting tools sort spending into categories automatically instead of leaving customers to do it themselves. None of this is glamorous, but it's the sort of friction reduction that shapes how people feel about a service long after they've forgotten which feature caused it.
Entertainment has followed a similar path, just with more visible results. Where a streaming platform once built its whole library around what was popular nationally, it's now far more common to see individually curated homepages, genre-based discovery tools, and algorithms trying to second-guess a mood rather than a category. The logic holds across sectors: don't make the user go looking for what they want, try to have it ready before they ask.
Familiarity Doesn't Always Mean Trust
None of this means Irish consumers have simply welcomed AI driven personalisation without question, though. The Central Statistics Office's Trust Survey 2025, carried out as part of the OECD's international Trust Survey, found that 56% of people felt they understood AI well enough to explain it to someone else, with a further 42% saying they had at least a general idea.
Familiarity, in other words, is high. But the same research turned up something more cautionary: roughly half of respondents weren't confident that government agencies could use AI to tailor services to individuals without the results feeling unfair or poorly handled, and a clear majority had doubts about how their personal data would be protected in the process.
That gap between high familiarity and more measured trust is worth sitting with, because it probably applies just as much to commercial AI as it does to public services. People seem increasingly happy to let an algorithm recommend a film or flag a suspicious transaction. They're considerably less relaxed about a black box deciding what they see, what they pay, or how their behaviour is being read, without any real sense of how or why.
A separate CSO survey found that 42% of Irish internet users had used generative AI in the previous three months, rising to 65% among 16- to 29-year-olds, so this is a country where younger users especially have grown up expecting technology to adapt to them. Whether that expectation extends to trusting how it's actually done is a different question altogether.
The Trade-Off Consumers Are Actually Making
That's really the fault line running through all of this. Consumers want convenience and relevance, but they also want some visibility into how it's produced: what's being collected, how long it's kept, and whether they can switch it off if they'd rather not be profiled at all. Companies that explain, even briefly, why a recommendation is being made tend to fare better on trust than ones that simply present the result and move on. The gap between "here's why you're seeing this" and total silence on the matter does a lot of work in how comfortable people end up feeling.
Where this goes next probably depends less on the technology itself, which will likely keep improving quietly in the background, and more on how transparently it's rolled out. Ireland's new AI Office, established this summer under the Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Act 2026, and the wider EU AI Act obligations phasing in through the rest of the year, suggest regulators are alive to exactly this tension.
For consumers, the practical result by the end of 2026 is likely to be more personalisation across e-commerce, streaming, banking and entertainment, but delivered alongside clearer opt-outs and plainer explanations than the first wave of AI-powered features managed. Given how quickly Irish consumers have taken to AI already, that combination of convenience and clarity may end up mattering more than any single new feature.

items.body:
One day in 2007, Darren Sudlow drove past the old stationmaster’s house at Padgate station, in Cheshire, noticed it was empty and decided to lease it. “He just fell in love with the place,” says his son, Kieran, who was 11 at the time. “He said he always wanted a fish and chip shop, for some reason.” Despite having worked as a joiner up to that point, Darren made a go of it, and the Plaice Station, as he named it, was a success from day one. “He worked like mad to get it open and then realised that the hard work hadn’t even started, and he had a queue out the door,” says the younger Sudlow.
The family lived nearby. Kieran Sudlow, who is now 30, worked at the Plaice Station as a boy, peeling potatoes, washing dishes after school, then cooking at the range when he was 16. He went on to become a chef, working in Australia for a few years, then returning to help out at the chippy part-time when needed. Business had always been pretty good. They won local awards and had a loyal customer base. But one day in March, Kieran remembers, his father came in and told him: “‘I think the fish and chip shop’s going to go.’ He said, ‘It’s not making money. I can’t see it carrying on.’”
In April, after 19 years, the Plaice Station served its last customer. In a Facebook post, Darren Sudlow explained that the closure was the result of multiple pressures: “Soaring fish prices, reduced fishing quotas and political issues around the world, relentless demands on VAT among other ever-increasing expenses, effectively destroying any profit margins remaining. Truth is, the product of fish and chips itself is facing its toughest battle.”
Chippies across the UK are feeling similarly pessimistic. According to research carried out in May by the National Federation of Fish Friers (NFFF), 47% of them were “extremely worried” about the future of their business, and a further 30% were “slightly worried”. About 20% of them planned to quit in the next 12 months. Many have already shut in recent years. There are still 7,000-8,000 chippies in Britain, down from a peak of 25,000 in the 1930s, but the number of outlets, and the number of servings, are shrinking weekly. The big chains are also feeling the pressure: Deep Blue, which owns the historic Harry Ramsden’s brand, shut down nine of its restaurants last summer.
Customers cannot have failed to notice the problem. The average price of takeaway fish and chips has gone up more than 60% in the past five years, from about £7 to £11.43 – a faster rise than other takeaway foods. A family of four would now pay nearly £50 for their meal. “It’s a fair chunk of money and I think it’s shocked people a little bit,” says Andrew Crook, president of the NFFF. “So they cut back on the number of visits, so volumes are going down as well.”
Crook has been feeling it himself; he runs two chippies in Lancashire, and has been in the trade for 27 years. The recent hot weather has been good for coastal outlets, but “if you’re inland, nobody wants fish and chips”, he says. It’s been a hard summer for shops like his. “It’s not a very pleasant place to be when it’s hot, and it’s quiet as well. The night drags, and it can be 40-50C in the shop.”
These are difficult times for UK hospitality across the board, but chippy owners have it particularly tough, Crook explains. For starters, they’re beholden to the costs of a very small set of basic ingredients. Fish prices have risen astronomically in recent years, especially cod and haddock. The cod quota in the Barents Sea, where most of the fish comes from, has gone down from about 1m tonnes in 2020 to just 285,000 tonnes this year, according to Undercurrent, a seafood industry data company. Inevitably, this has pushed up prices. “For an 18kg case of cod [fillets], I was paying something like £160 three years ago, and I’m now paying £330,” says Crook. Haddock quotas are slightly less affected, but the scarcity of cod has created a knock-on demand, again affecting prices.
The Ukraine war has also had an impact on the industry (hence the “political issues” Darren Sudlow was referring to). The Barents Sea is jointly managed by Norway and Russia, but in May 2025, the EU sanctioned two Russian fishing companies, Murman SeaFood and the giant Norebo JSC, over alleged surveillance and sabotage activities. That has disrupted the whole supply chain, again raising prices.
Potato prices are also likely to rise: after the heatwaves and droughts, this year’s European harvest will be one of the worst on record. Even cooking oil prices are going up. Then there are energy costs: the range has to be kept hot, and a lot of freezing and refrigeration is required. And the equipment is not cheap: a new frying range can cost upwards of £10,000.
On the administrative side, chippies have been hit hard by recent rises in VAT (it returned to 20% in April 2022, after a temporary reduction during the pandemic to 5% and then 12.5%), business rates, the minimum wage and mandatory sick pay. The government has been putting in relief measures – lowering business rates for pubs and clubs in England, capping VAT on children’s meals over the summer – but none of this benefits chippies, says Crook. “So it does feel like we’re being run by our business now, rather than running the business. It’s taken a lot of the fun out of it for many.”
All of these factors hit the Plaice Station, says Kieran Sudlow, squeezing margins tighter and tighter. VAT was the last straw. Like many small businesses, the firm was paying a flat rate of 12.5% to the government, but in 2025 its accountant warned it was approaching a limit: if the business’s annual turnover exceeded £230,000, the flat rate would no longer apply. “So it was going to cost us tens of thousands of pounds.”
The only option was to earn less money. The Sudlows made the painful decision to temporarily close. “As strange as it sounds, we made more money by closing for three weeks than if we’d just stayed open,” Kieran says. In order to justify leaving the flat rate scheme, they would have had to turn over an extra £2,000 a week. “After 19 years, you know where you are with your business. You can’t just find an extra two grand a week.”
Closing down was a demoralising experience. “I felt we were doing everything we could to make the products as good as possible. But then all that work that you’ve done to grow your business is ripped out from under your feet.”
There’s another factor at play here: changing tastes. Fish and chips has been facing stiff competition from other takeaway options: pizzas, burgers, fried chicken, Indian, Chinese, Korean – most of which use much cheaper ingredients. Deep-fried foods are also losing popularity for health reasons, since they contribute to obesity; the government recently banned them from schools in England.
Fish and chips is a great British institution, but the origins of the dish are not all that deep, or that British. The technique of coating fish in flour and deep-frying it is thought to have been introduced by Jewish immigrants from Spain and Portugal in the 17th century, but fish and chips only caught on commercially in the mid-19th century (starting in either London or Lancashire – it’s disputed). In the days before British cuisine opened up to international influences, it was one of the few convenience foods. It was also one of the few meals not rationed during the second world war, further cementing its patriotic connotations.
One chip shop owner in his 80s (who did not wish to be named, as he is in the process of selling up) recalls starting out in the business in his 20s, in a small town in the north of England. “It was pretty busy, because in those days there was only your chip shop and your butcher’s and your pie shop,” he says. For most of his career it was a good way to make a living. His wife and children helped out in his shops and they often lived above the premises. But it has been tougher in recent years, he agrees, and he’s struggling to find a buyer for his business. Today’s establishments don’t look that different from the ones he started out in: “They’re more modern and very good-looking, but other than that, they haven’t changed. They can’t, because you can’t change the way you cook fish and chips.”
The unchanging nature of fish and chips is both its strength and its weakness. Kieran Sudlow had begun to notice the dish falling out of fashion: “You’ve got a very ageing market – your traditionalists, your mums, your dads, your nans, they grew up on fish and chips. But we could see clear as day, and especially now with online orders and social media posts, your 18- to 35-year-olds, that younger bracket that’s your next generation of customers, they’re not interacting. They’re not coming through the doors.”
A lot of chippies have tried using different, cheaper fish, such as hake, plaice, rock or spurdog (types of dogfish), or even tilapia, a freshwater fish farmed in southeast Asia. Many chippies claim customers would not be able to tell the difference, but we’re wedded to cod and haddock. Other chippies have expanded their menus to include items such as calamari, fishcakes, fried chicken, sausages, kebabs or loaded chips.
Sudlow decided to change tack entirely. Three months after the Plaice Station closed, he reopened as Between Bread, a high-end sandwich shop. The fare is a cut above: he uses locally sourced “shokupan”, or Japanese milk bread; fillings include braised beef with chipotle sauce, and spicy tuna and avocado; prices are between £8 and £12. He did his homework, researching food trends and visiting similar establishments around the country. Business is great, he says – turnover is “much higher” than when it was a chippy ((justifying that VAT change), and the shop is popular on social media and with young people. He also gets to be a bit more creative as a chef. Does he miss the chippy days?
“Personally, no,” he says. “It got to a point at the end where it really was like fighting. It’s an expensive product to buy in nowadays and even harder to sell. Staff training is a nightmare: how many people do you know that go, ‘When I grow up I want to cook fish and chips’? It’s a part-time job; staff turnover’s horrendous. It’s a hard business to have.”
But the great British chippy is not to be written off just yet. Cod and haddock quotas are expected to increase 10% next year, says Undercurrent, which could help reduce prices, and the UK government is facing increasing pressure to deal with the VAT problems plaguing the hospitality industry.
Most importantly, perhaps, a new generation is embracing the chippy tradition and breathing new life into it – not necessarily by totally transforming it, but by doing it simply and well. The Scrap Box, outside York, is one such example: it won best takeaway this year at the NFFF’s National Fish & Chip awards.
The Scrap Box was founded 12 years ago by brothers Aman and Gavin Dhesi, aged 37 and 33. Sons of a local off-licence keeper, they studied politics and economics at university, respectively, but then decided to open a chippy together. “It was pretty much on a whim, to be honest,” says Aman. “I was never proud to be doing fish and chips and never felt like it was really me.” After Covid, the brothers reached a crossroads, he continues. “It was like – do we do something else, do we sell out, or do we really double down and go on a journey to try to make sure we can improve every single aspect of the business?”
They went on the journey, researching every aspect of the trade and its history, carefully sourcing their supplies and “letting our ingredients do the talking”: their fish comes from Iceland and is Marine Stewardship Council-certified; they fry in beef dripping from Ireland. There’s no secret formula, Aman says. The fish is lightly seasoned; the batter is just flour and water and a bit of natural colouring, applied as thinly as possible. Nothing artificial is added. “The main thing is, it needs to be made often, as opposed to just all done in the morning, so that it retains its bubbles and you still get your spikiness. And it wants to be cold, so that when it hits the oil, it has a bigger reaction – you get a nicer texture.”
When I visit on a Friday night, the Scrap Box – a roadside hut on a layby that used to be a council toilet block – is buzzing: six or seven people cooking at a huge range; a constant bustle of customers. The menu is classic: haddock and chips for £11.95, cod and chips a pound more, sides like curry sauce and mushy peas, a few non-fish options. And the food is everything you’d want it to be: the fish fresh and succulent, the batter crisp and light, the chips hot and sog-free.
At the end of the shift, Gavin tells me they’ve done about 650 portions that night. The award has raised their profile. They’ve just returned from a trip to see the fishing in Iceland, he says, and they’re about to go to Japan, where they’re doing pop-up stores in three cities. “There’s been so many opportunities – that’s kept us stimulated and excited.” They’re also looking at opening a branch in London, Aman says: “We want to bring the best of the north to the south.”
Despite the union-jack-waving seaside cliches, what makes fish and chips quintessentially British is that it’s interwoven with our history of immigration and internationalism, says Aman, whose family has Punjabi roots. It is often immigrants who have run British chippies, he points out: Italians in Scotland, Chinese in Liverpool and the north-west of England, Indians and Pakistanis, Greeks and Turks. The fish recipe came from Sephardic Jews in Portugal; the potatoes often come from central Europe (via South America); the fish comes from Iceland and Norway.
There are other outlets doing similar things to the Scrap Box around the UK. In Nottinghamshire the Cod’s Scallops (corny names come with the territory) includes fresh fish counters in its outlets; in Oxford Harrisons’s Fish & Chip Co has been diversifying its menu with a range of British fish. There are new young proprietors of established family chippies trying new things, and there are food trucks and mobile chippies such as Frosty’s in Northumberland keeping prices down by minimising their premises.
So maybe there’s life in the old chippy yet. “I do think the better shops will survive and prosper,” says Aman Dhesi. “But it’s never going to die out.” Gavin agrees: “I think we need to hark back to just how pure a dish it is, how great it is. And when you think about it, for where it’s come from and the work that’s gone into it, it’s still a bargain.”

items.title: Natwest chair: Boost investment in UK or risk ‘inter-generational crisis’
items.summary: The chair of Natwest has warned the UK is in a “moment of national crisis” that can only be fixed by firing up investment in the country’s flagging economy. Rick Haythornthwaite, the City grandee who has also chaired the boards of Mastercard and Ocado, told City AM that years of political instability and poor decision-making [...]
items.body:
Natwest chair: Boost investment in UK or risk ‘inter-generational crisis’
The chair of Natwest has warned the UK is in a “moment of national crisis” that can only be fixed by firing up investment in the country’s flagging economy.
Rick Haythornthwaite, the City grandee who has also chaired the boards of Mastercard and Ocado, told City AM that years of political instability and poor decision-making have hampered public and private sector investment and kneecapped Britain’s growth prospects.
“Where we’re headed right now is into a very, very difficult national debt situation, into an inter-generational crisis and to lives on the street that are increasingly difficult,” he said. “These are all things that need to be confronted now.”
Haythornthwaite made the intervention to mark the launch of a fresh report from the 2030 Prosperity Alliance sounding the alarm on the chronic underinvestment in the UK economy. ‘Neglect’ – the first in a five-part series of papers taking on “giants that stand in the way of economic growth” – warns that over the past three decades the average G7 economy has invested £2 trillion more than the UK.
The alliance is led by Haythornthwaite and boasts the chairs of Diageo, National Grid, Barratt Redrow and Reckitt as members. In Neglect, it singled out the “thicket of rules and regulation” and a national aversion to risk as responsible for the dearth of animal spirits in the UK.
It added that inconsistent political messages and the proliferation of watchdogs and legal process also needed to be “slayed” if the UK wants to match the dynamism of other major economies.
Britain’s £2 trillion investment gap
Authors estimated that even if investment levels in the UK rose by four per cent a year, it would take a century for the country to close the £2 trillion ‘investment gap‘ between it and peers like the US, France and Japan.
The paper was unveiled just weeks before John Healey delivers his maiden Budget against a bleak fiscal and monetary backdrop. Growth has outstripped expectations for much of this year, but the re-escalation of the Middle East conflict and persistently high government borrowing has left the Chancellor hemmed in by his self-imposed spending rules.
At the speech – slated for 28 October – Healey is expected to use a carve-out to those rules that allows greater borrowing for investment, the proceeds from which will be allocated to what are known as Public Financial Institutions (PuFins).
Haythornthwaite said the bodies, which include the British Business Bank and National Wealth Fund, could “undoubtedly play a role” to help bridge the investment gap. “They need to be clear in their mandates, they need to be very joined up in their thinking [and] they need more scale than they have right now,” he added.
But the City doyenne said the majority of investment must come from businesses if Britain is to make up the ground it has ceded to peers. A slew of recent macroeconomic shocks like the pandemic and the Iran war has caused firms across the UK to put investment plans on ice. But 2030 Prosperity Alliance’s paper – ring-led by former Institute of Fiscal Studies chief Paul Johnson – found the lion’s share of issues deterring private sector investment to have come from self-inflicted issues like regulation and the country’s febrile politics.
“The private sector has to step up as well,” Haythornthwaite said, citing the fact British firms have historically invested more in branding and market research than research and development. “This is about business partnering with whatever government is of the day. But to do that, business has to be able to price the future. And if you’re pricing the future you need stability and predictability [which] is not something that has been enjoyed in recent times.”
